vignette:
Patient: Robert, 55-year-old male, European, single, employed as a counselor at a community mental health center.
Trauma: Man-made disaster (industrial explosion at a manufacturing plant)
PCL-5 Score: 74 (severe)

Robert arrives for his sessions precisely on time, often with a cup of coffee that he holds but rarely drinks. He is a tall man with a quiet, measured way of speaking, the kind of voice that has been trained to soothe others. He works as a counselor at a community mental health center, a job he has held for twenty-two years. His colleagues describe him as "steady," "a rock." Robert says he feels like a fraud.

The event that changed everything happened fourteen months ago. Robert was not at the plant. He was at his office, fifteen miles away, leading a weekly grief support group. He remembers the sound-a low, percussive thump that rattled the windows. He remembers the fluorescent lights flickering, the way the ceiling tiles shifted. He told the group it was probably construction. He kept his voice calm. He was the therapist. He was supposed to hold the room.

It was only later, during his lunch break, that he saw the news. A chemical explosion at the Apex Manufacturing plant on the east side of the city. The blast had leveled a four-block radius. He watched the footage on his phone, standing in the break room. The smoke was black and thick, boiling into the sky. The reporter said there were fatalities. Robert felt his hands go cold. He had no connection to the plant. He did not know anyone who worked there. But he could not stop watching the loop of the gray building collapsing into itself.

That night, he could not sleep. He lay in bed, replaying the thump. He felt the vibration in his chest, over and over. He started to think about the people inside. He imagined them at their desks, maybe drinking coffee, maybe thinking about their evening plans. He imagined the moment the walls came down. He could not stop the images.

In the weeks that followed, Robert began to change in ways he did not fully recognize. He stopped watching the news. He stopped driving past the east side of the city entirely, taking a longer route to work. He started checking the exits in every room he entered-the grocery store, the movie theater, his own office. He would scan the ceiling for cracks, listen for strange sounds. He became hyperaware of the hum of the building's HVAC system. He told himself it was just vigilance. He was a counselor. He knew about hypervigilance. He knew the word. But knowing the word did not stop his heart from racing when a truck backfired in the parking lot.

His work suffered. He found it harder to sit with his clients' stories. A man describing a car accident made Robert's palms sweat. A woman talking about a house fire made him feel like he could not breathe. He began to dissociate during sessions, his mind drifting to the black smoke, the collapsing wall. He would nod and say "that sounds difficult" on autopilot. He felt hollow. He started canceling appointments, citing migraines. He has taken more sick days in the last year than in the previous ten combined.

Socially, he has retreated. He used to enjoy Friday dinners with a small group of friends from graduate school. Now he makes excuses. The restaurant is too crowded. The noise is too loud. He feels exposed in public, like the ceiling could fall at any moment. He has not been on a date in over a year. He tells himself he is too tired.

At night, the dreams come. They are not about the explosion itself. They are about the moments after. He dreams he is standing in the rubble, and he can hear people calling for help, but he cannot find them. He wakes up gasping, his sheets soaked, his heart hammering. He does not go back to sleep. He sits in the dark and waits for dawn.

Robert is a man who has spent his entire adult life helping people hold their pain. He is now discovering that his own pain has a weight he cannot carry alone. He does not know how to be the patient. He does not know how to tell his colleagues that the rock is crumbling.
